input.verdict: Weak support. Hematite is an absorber at 2.7 eV (MEGNet PBE gap 1.53, which underestimates; the real gap is about 2.1). The measurements show EQE falling steeply from Fe-rich (0.108%) to FeSbO4 (0.005%), so the best region is the hematite-rich end. Index 3 (Fe 0.79) tests whether a local optimum exists below index 0's Sb level. MEGNet can't tell apart these doping levels, so on that question the model is uninformative.

content.text:
I submitted **index 0** (Fe 0.84 / Sb 0.16) as the best composition. Its EQE of 0.108% was the highest of the three I measured, but I don't know how it compares with the library's best.

| Index | Fe fraction | EQE (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.84 | 0.108 |
| 3 | 0.79 | 0.053 |
| 13 | 0.52 (near FeSbO4) | 0.005 |

- **Trend:** EQE falls steadily as Sb rises. This fits Sb-doped hematite doing the light absorption at the 2.7 eV illumination.
- **FeSbO4 (index 13):** the models predicted it is stable with a 2.08 eV gap, so it should absorb, but it performed poorly.
- **Sb-rich end:** I didn't measure it. It should hold the FeSb2O6 phase, which the models predict is stable with a narrow 1.28 eV gap, and EQE was already falling as Sb increased.

The main risk is that index 0 is the most Fe-rich composition on the line, so the peak could lie at even lower Sb than the library covers. Index 1 or 2 could also be slightly better; I spent the last measurement on index 3 because a result there would say more about the trend. I didn't use any of the 5 XRD measurements, so the phase assignments rest on the list of known structures and the model predictions, not on diffraction data.
